html:
The Adena culture was a group of related Native American societies of the Ohio Valley from about 500 BCE to 100 CE, in the Early Woodland period. They are known for burial mounds. Their heartland was southern Ohio, and they reached into Kentucky, West Virginia, Indiana and Pennsylvania.

The name comes from the Adena estate near Chillicothe, Ohio, where a mound was dug in 1901. Adena people hunted, fished and gathered, grew local seed plants of the Eastern Agricultural Complex, and made pottery. They buried important dead in log tombs and heaped earth over them, adding new burials over generations until some mounds grew very large, like the Grave Creek Mound in West Virginia. They traded for copper and shells and carved stone smoking pipes.

They came after the Poverty Point earthworks to the south, and were followed by the Hopewell culture, which carried mound building and trade much further. Both grew out of the world of the eastern woodland peoples.
